tasks.source_read: PMC full text PMC6137521 (read by AI reader 187: all sections, Key Points, the Table, the counts in Figure 1 and the legends of Figures 1 to 3; the supplement not read)
tasks.extracted: Studies requiring more than 72 hours of abstinence before testing (k = 15; n = 928) found d −0.08 (95% CI −0.22 to 0.07; P = .29), smaller than studies requiring 72 hours or less, none included (k = 54; n = 7,799; d −0.30, −0.37 to −0.22); chi-square 6.36, P = .01. Longer mean reported abstinence (k = 28; n = 1,661) went with smaller differences (beta 0.059; P = .04, uncorrected; unit of the beta not stated). Figure 3 also plots the studies requiring no abstinence (k = 22) and 1 to 72 hours (k = 32) separately, to show that the zero or unknown abstinence studies do not drive the difference. A comparison between studies, not a change within the same people; the more-than-72-hours interval includes no difference and reaches −0.22, close to the overall estimate of −0.25, which lies just outside it.

tasks.source_read: PMC full text PMC7646282 (Lancet Psychiatry 6(5):427-436; Tables 1 to 3 as text, Figures 1 to 3 read on screen; appendix not read)
tasks.extracted: 901 people with first-episode psychosis and 1,237 population controls at 11 sites. Daily use (the most consistent lifetime pattern) was reported by 266 cases (29.5%) and 84 controls (6.8%). Against never or occasional use (1,061 controls, 528 cases): daily use, odds ratio 6.2 (4.8 to 8.2) adjusted for age, gender and ethnicity, and 3.2 (2.2 to 4.1) fully adjusted (adding education, employment, tobacco, stimulants, ketamine, legal highs and hallucinogens), p < 0.0001; use more than once a week 2.5 (1.9 to 3.5) and 1.4 (1.0 to 2.0). Ever use against never use: 2.45 (2.0 to 2.9) and 1.3 (1.1 to 1.6). The abstract describes the daily-use comparison as against never use (first reader's reporting issue).

tasks.extracted: The Methods say never use was always the reference, but Table 1's reference rows include no cannabis within the last year (Wiles et al.), no cannabis use at age 18 (Arseneault et al.) and none or no use for frequency at baseline (Henquet et al.; Degenhardt and Hall). Swedish conscripts of 1969 (ref. 15, Zammit et al., 2002), inpatient admission for schizophrenia (ICD-8 and ICD-9) by lifetime frequency of use at conscription: 215 cases among 36,429 men who had never used cannabis and 28 among 731 who had used it more than 50 times (crude odds ratio 6.71); follow-up length not stated in this source. Editors' calculation: crude proportions 0.59% (about 6 in 1,000) and 3.8% (about 38 in 1,000), nothing adjusted. Five of the six pooled cohorts are the reports that Moore et al. (2007) also pooled (Tien and Anthony 1990, ECA; Arseneault 2002, Dunedin; Zammit 2002, Swedish conscripts; Henquet 2005, EDSP; Wiles 2006, NPMS; editors' cross-check of the two reference lists).

tasks.locator: Summary › Findings; Methods › Measures, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 2, rows Lifetime cannabis use and Lifetime use of cannabis by potency; Results, 3rd and 9th paragraphs; Figure 1 (value labels); Discussion, 2nd paragraph; reference 28
tasks.source_read: PMC full text PMC7646282 (Lancet Psychiatry 6(5):427-436): text from AI reader 216's saved copy, read by the adjudicator; Figure 1 viewed in the adjudicator's own browser tab on 2026-10-31
tasks.extracted: 901 cases and 1,237 population controls at 11 sites, recruited between May 1, 2010, and April 1, 2015. Questions on the type of cannabis made no reference to potency; potency was assigned from THC concentrations by type in a 2016 European report, supplemented by national data. The main text speaks of lifetime use of cannabis by potency, not of the type mainly used: in Table 2 every person who had used is in one potency class (331 + 240 = 571 of 574 controls, potency missing for 3; 251 + 334 = 585 cases; editors' arithmetic). Against never use, fully adjusted (Figure 1): occasional use 0.84 (THC below 10%) and 0.96 (10% or more), use more than once a week 1.36 and 1.57, daily use 2.19 and 4.78, the text giving 2.2 (1.4 to 3.6) and 4.8 (2.5 to 6.3); no evidence of interaction between frequency of use and type (p = 0.25). The authors present the daily high-potency finding as a replication of their previous south London study (ref. 28, Di Forti et al., 2015).

tasks.source_read: PMC full text PMC5984096 (Molecular Psychiatry 23(5):1287-1292): Abstract and Discussion read in the adjudicator's own browser tab on 2026-10-31
tasks.extracted: The authors write that the genetic approach strongly supports the hypothesis that cannabis use is causally related to the risk of schizophrenia, and call it additional evidence that cannabis use is likely to increase that risk; the abstract prints P = 0.007, the p-value of the per-unit estimate, beside the rescaled odds ratio of 1.37 for people who use against people who do not. They note that the variants did not reach genome-wide significance and that, with non-overlapping exposure and outcome data, weak-instrument bias would bias the estimate towards the null.

tasks.locator: Abstract › Conclusions; Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion › Strengths and limitations, 2nd, 5th and 7th paragraphs; Conclusion, 1st paragraph
tasks.source_read: PMC full text PMC5341491 (Psychological Medicine 47(5):971-980): Abstract, Discussion, Strengths and limitations and Conclusion read in the adjudicator's own browser tab on 2026-10-31
tasks.extracted: The authors read their results as some evidence that cannabis initiation increases the risk of schizophrenia, with a small causal estimate and any effect of initiation likely to be small, and as strong, stronger, evidence that schizophrenia risk predicts initiation, adding that the weakness of the cannabis instrument limits interpretation. Limitations they state: large overlap between exposure and outcome samples would bias results towards the observational association; the reverse analysis assumes that genetic predictors of schizophrenia act in the general population, most of whom never develop it; MR-Egger tests direct (biological) pleiotropy, not mediated pleiotropy; and a genetic correlation fits shared genetic architecture or causation in either direction.
